1:
The psalm is recognised at once as a different kind of thing. Delitzsch calls it a psalm of nature such as no Gentile poet could have written: the Israelite stands free before nature, and all things appear as brought forth and sustained by one God, good in themselves and disordered only by man's self-corruption. Where the psalm before sang God's rule in the kingdom of grace, this sings his rule in nature, following the order of Genesis. Calvin marks the same difference: this one neither treats of the benefits bestowed on the church nor lifts us to the hope of heaven, but presents a lively image of wisdom, power and goodness in the order of nature. He also quotes a judgement of its form — perhaps the principal poem in the collection; older than the Exodus, since it alludes neither to the Mosaic ritual nor to the deliverance from Egypt; and sung alternately by two companies, one speaking of God in the third person and the other addressing him in the second.

Clarke supplies the title. There is none in the Hebrew or Chaldee, but the ancient versions give it to David, the Greek heading it a psalm concerning the formation of the world and the Syriac making it his when he went with the priests to adore before the ark. It seems a continuation of the psalm before, and nine of Kennicott's and De Rossi's manuscripts write it as part of it. Spurgeon notices the same kinship: the psalm begins and ends like its predecessor, and a perfect model deserves to exist in duplicate. He also notes that thou art very great, being the natural deduction from a survey of the universe, would have been in place at the end; standing first, it shows the psalm was digested before it was written.

The robe of light is worked hard by all of them. Clarke reports that all the imagery of the exordium seems drawn from the tabernacle: the verb rendered put on is the word used of the clothing of the priests, and the word rendered curtain denotes the tabernacle's own curtains. Ellicott prefers the participles, putting on light as a robe, spreading the heavens as a curtain, because the psalmist thinks of light not as a single past act but as a continued operation: light is the dress of divinity, the ethereal woof God is for ever weaving for his own wear. The curtain he takes as a tent's, the Hebrew expressing the tremulous movement of its folds; he reports the explanations offered — the curtains of the Holy of Holies, or a surviving nomadic instinct — but sees no need to limit so natural a figure.

Henry organises the whole passage as a royal progress. Princes appear great in their robes, and God's robes are honour and majesty; in their palaces, and he stretches the heavens like a curtain and lays the beams of his chambers in the waters; in their coaches of state, and he makes the clouds his chariots and walks a stately pace on the wings of the wind; and in their retinue, and his are the angels. Beside this the equipage of eastern kings is as a glow-worm's light to the sun. Gill and Wesley take the light for the first created light, Gill adding that it expresses God's own nature and belongs to Christ, of whose glory the transfiguration was an emblem. Calvin turns the figure into an argument: in his essence God dwells in light inaccessible, but since he irradiates the world by his splendour, that is the garment in which he who is hidden appears visible to us. Augustine allegorises — the light is the church, made light in him though darkness in herself, and the heaven stretched like a skin is the authority of Scripture, a skin because it signifies mortality, the writings having been dispensed through mortal men.
3:
The chambers laid in the waters are architecture. Ellicott says the Hebrew verb is the exact equivalent of the Latin for framing timbers together, and the chambers are lofts or upper stories; the pavilion God rears rests on a floor of rain-clouds, like a tent on a roof. Clarke finds the same figure in the tabernacle, kept together by a perpetual jointing of its parts, and adds that the seat of the divine presence, moving with the ark on a cloud, is called by the sacred historians the Chariot. Ellicott derives the word from a parallel psalm, where chariot stands in place of cherub, and takes the wings of the wind from clouds floating like drifted wings.

The fourth verse produces the sharpest disagreement here. Ellicott reverses the Authorised Version: rather who maketh winds his messengers, a flaming fire his ministers, since the context deals throughout with the divine King's use of natural forces — as the clouds are a chariot and the sky a tent, so the winds are messengers and the lightnings servants. He concedes that the verse alone favours the interpretation adopted in the Epistle to the Hebrews, the traditional Jewish reading; but the context sets it aside, Hebrew poets arranging their words with comparative indifference to order. Gill keeps the received sense and argues that Christ, by whom the angels were made, is greater than they; some, he adds, render it as the winds, to which angels may be compared for invisibility and speed. Wesley agrees that they are incorporeal, the fitter for their employments, and called fire for their force. Clarke takes the other side: the elements are prompt to perform the divine commands like ministers serving in the tabernacle.

On the founding of the earth Clarke again sees the tabernacle, so laid that nothing could move it; sanctuary and earth are sometimes described in the same words. Ellicott prefers he fixed the earth on its foundations, and meets the objection: that this contradicts the passage in Job which hangs the earth upon nothing need cause no difficulty, both being poetical, not scientific. He adds that the verse gave the Inquisition an argument against Galileo. Gill canvasses the candidates for the bases — waters, centre of gravity, mountains, air — and settles on the power of God. Wesley states the wonder physically: God has fixed so strange a place for a heavy body that one would think it should fall every moment, yet whichever way it stirred it must fall upwards, and can be ruined only by tumbling into heaven.

The covering deep is read as the first state of things, not the flood. Gill says so expressly, and Ellicott adds a point of weight: the idea of a chaos finds no place here, the primitive world being not formless but having its mountains and valleys already, merged beneath the sea. Delitzsch calls it the primordial mass in which the earth lay as in embryo, and holds that the earth, hanging free in space, has internal supports and will come out of the predicted judgment glorified. When the waters flee, Spurgeon has them behave like intelligent agents hurrying to their appointed deeps: by that same word shall the floods of trouble be restrained. Their going up by the mountains divides them again. Clarke doubts water could ascend through fissures to a summit and run down, preferring rain stopped by strata, or vapours condensed above. Ellicott calls the received rendering grammatically possible but inconsistent, and makes hills and valleys the subjects — hills rise, valleys sink — anticipating, in a different sense, geology. On the bound Clarke names the flux and reflux of the sea, the lunar attraction, the earth's rotation and gravitation, and behind them God's will; Ellicott hears the Hebrew dread of the sea, for which the coast is neither recreation nor commerce but the defence God has set against hostile waters.
10:
Springs open the section. Clarke works from evaporation: God has apportioned the watery surface to the dry and the solar attraction to both, and experiments show the proportion needed is about seventeen to three, the proportion the sea bears to the land. Henry admits the naturalists dispute the origin of fountains, but says that whatever the second causes, this is the first: there is water enough in the sea to drown us but not a drop to refresh us, it is all so salt. Ellicott notices what the psalm does that Genesis does not. Genesis passes abruptly from dry land to the vegetation covering it, with no physical means for its production, whereas an Oriental poet thinks first of the springs on which life depends, and in sympathy with nature hastens, against the original record, to people his world with creatures who share the Creator's joy.

The wild ass gets unusual attention. Clarke describes it as differing from the tame ass only in that its spirit is unbroken, so swift that no horse but the Arab barb can overtake it, and so jealous of its liberty that it retires deep into the desert — yet even there springs are provided. Henry makes the point morally: the wild asses, untameable and so of no use to man, are welcome to quench their thirst, and we have no reason to grudge it them. Wesley is blunter: stupid creatures, yet plentifully provided for. On the birds Clarke says all fowls love verdure and reside where they can find wood and water; Ellicott corrects the preposition to above them, in the trees on the bank.

The three gifts of the fifteenth verse draw Clarke's best writing. Wine in moderate quantity revives; ardent spirits exhilarate but exhaust the strength, and every dose leaves a man the worse, whereas unadulterated wine makes him cheerful and continues that cheerfulness by strengthening the muscles and bracing the nerves. Those who drink till it inflames them abuse the mercy. Oil is for anointing the parts most exposed to sun and weather, since by it the pores are kept open. Hunger prostrates not only the strength but the natural courage, yet a little bread restores it before it can have been prepared for nutriment, an effect he says has not been satisfactorily accounted for. In the germination of a grain of wheat, he adds, there is a profusion of miracles. Ellicott re-punctuates so that the wine makes the face shine more than oil, and notes that the verb rendered strengthen properly means props. Wesley refers the oil to the custom of anointing the face at festivals. Gill turns the wine into a figure of the love of God and the joys of heaven.

The trees of the Lord are agreed to be trees no man planted. Clarke asks who ever sowed the seeds of the cedars of Lebanon, or of the thousands of forests on the globe, and answers that God sowed them and they flourished without the care of man. Ellicott says the cedar was the grandest tree known to the Hebrew, honoured like lightning and the tropical rain with the epithet of grandeur; such trees must have been planted by the divine hand, since man could grow herbs but not cedars. Clarke suggests the heron for the birds nesting highest, but Ellicott defends the stork, which readily selects a fir as the tallest convenient tree near its feeding-grounds. On the last creatures Clarke draws the lesson that the barren hilltops and craggy precipices are not without their uses, no part of the creation being useless and its inhabitants necessary links in the chain of animated beings. Gill derives the Hebrew for the wild goats from climbing, and observes that a wild goose chase should properly be a wild goat's; Ellicott identifies the animal with the ibex and the cony with the hyrax, whose Hebrew name means hider.
19:
Why the moon is named before the sun is asked by all. Delitzsch says the poet has the order of the creation days before his mind and puts the moon first so the picture of day may follow that of night, the moon being the calendrical principal star. Ellicott gives the same two reasons, the calendar and the reckoning that makes evening and morning a day. Gill reports the Jewish explanation that the night was before the day, and lists what the moon measures: months and years, the tides, and the appointed festivals. Clarke and Henry both turn the verse against the worship of the luminaries: the heathen thought them gods, and the psalm shows they are creatures dependent on God and made for man's use. Scripture takes all occasions, Henry says, to show that these gods are servants of the true God.

Ellicott makes the sharpest comparison with Genesis. There the heavenly bodies are made in what he calls a scientific manner, the lamps of heaven hung out at command; in the poem they move to their office like living things conscious of their glorious function. The sun is no mere mechanical timepiece but a conscious servant of God. Spurgeon reaches the same place devotionally: the moon's motions are never to be regarded as the result of impersonal law but as God's appointment, and the sun keeps his hour of going down to a second though it constantly varies — we need rousing in the morning, but he hides himself the instant the set time is come.

The division of night from day is read as a provision. Clarke says it is not God's design that there should be constant darkness or light: the sun gives man light to labour by, the night rest to recruit his strength; and since it would not suit man and the beasts to collect food at once, the night is given them for prey. When man labours they rest, and when man rests they labour. Henry adds an aesthetic note: darkness, though black, contributes to the beauty of nature and is a foil to the light of day, and under its protection the beasts creep forth as they dare not by daylight. Ellicott reads the return of morning as the psalm's great omission: the curse of labour on which Genesis dwells is out of sight, and in its place is the poetry of labour, the day bringing only healthy toil and the evening happy rest.

The lions are given natural history. Gill argues that they roar at the prey, when tearing and feeding on it, rather than before; but reports what naturalists say, that hunger makes their roar so hideous as to stupefy other creatures until they cannot stir, and that a jackal little bigger than a fox hunts the prey and holds it until the lion comes up. Young lions are named because their appetite is keenest, and the creature is an emblem of the adversary who goes about as a roaring lion. Clarke says the roar is so terrible as to unnerve the beast pursued, which though fleeter falls down.

The closing exclamation is heard as a change of key. Ellicott finds something as fine in art as true in religion in this sudden burst of praise at the day's close, an evening voluntary of grateful adoration; weariness leaves the soul as it is lifted from man's toil to God. Spurgeon presses the variety: not only many but manifold, works that abide the ages, works that perish in a year, works that do not outlive a day, works within works, and God the great ordainer of variety. Clarke finds three propositions — that the works are many and varied, that they show consummate wisdom in design and end, and that they are all God's property, whence he concludes that all abuse and waste of God's creatures is robbery upon the Creator.
25:
The turn to the sea is read as a moment of composition. Ellicott renders it yonder is the sea, great and broad, and imagines the poet on a hill-top commanding Lebanon on one hand and the Mediterranean on the other: lost in wonder, he had forgotten his Mosaic model, and the sight of water brings the words back. Clarke supposes the same more soberly, that the psalmist was within sight of the Mediterranean, and renders the Hebrew as great and extensive of hands, its waters like arms about the earth. Ellicott hears in the ships one accustomed to the navies of Phoenicia, an indication that the poet belonged to northern Palestine, and remarks that here for once we catch a breath of enthusiasm for the sea.

Leviathan divides them. Clarke allows the whale or any large marine animal, notes that the Greek and Latin call it a dragon, and takes the playing to mean that a sea uncontrollable in its surges is only a bowling-green to such monsters. Wesley says plainly the whale. Ellicott argues that in Job the creature is the crocodile but here is evidently of the sea, probably the whale; he reports also the rabbinical tradition that leviathan is God's plaything.

Every creature's dependence is then pressed. Clarke observes that God has furnished food suitable to every kind, and to each in its periods of growth, and that the opening hand alludes to scattering grain among fowls. On the hidden face Ellicott distinguishes: elsewhere the image means displeasure, here only withdrawal of providential care. He then draws out the psalm's view of death. Not the food only but the very breath of life is God's, to be sent forth or withdrawn at will; and death is to this poet neither sorrow nor mystery, since only the individual dies while the race lives, one generation fading as the breath is withdrawn and another succeeding. He warns against reading later doctrine into the word rendered spirit: it is breath, the power that gives matter a distinct but transient existence. Wesley says the same without the polemic — not the first creation but the continued production of living creatures. Gill refers it to the Holy Spirit and the succession of creatures in the room of those that die. Clarke goes the other way, asking whether the words do not imply a resurrection of the bodies that have been dissolved, and whether the brute creation is not principally intended.

On the divine rejoicing Henry contrasts ourselves: we often do what on review we wish undone, and we regret our bounty, but God always rejoices in his works because they are done in wisdom. Man's glory is fading and God's everlasting. Spurgeon says his works may pass away but not his glory. Ellicott notes that the poet still follows Genesis in showing God pleased with his finished work but says nothing of a sabbath.

The closing verses turn dark, and are met differently. Clarke makes the touch that kindles the hills a matter of volcanoes, and the trembling of the earth of the conflagration to come. Ellicott keeps it to awe: the world's existence depends on God's will, and a glance would shake it to its foundations. On the imprecation he offers a defence: since religion and patriotism were one in Israel, national feeling against heathen oppressors could hardly be absent from any hymn; but he presses further: the harmony of creation was broken by sin, and the song of creation would be false if no discord were heard in it. Gill restricts the sinners to the notorious; Clarke reads the clause as a prediction rather than a wish, that God shall consume the wicked till no more be found. Wesley notices that the closing word occurs here for the first time, on occasion of the destruction of the wicked, and last of all in the Revelation on a like one.
